As of 220 PM EDT Friday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Dry and relatively seasonable conditions are expected to 
prevail into the early portion of the weekend with high pressure 
overhead. Fair weather cumulus will wane towards this evening with 
clearing skies tonight. More cloud cover is possible in southeastern 
Vermont, associated with a departing coast low off the coast of 
southern New England. Temperatures tonight will be cooler across the 
northern and western locations falling into the upper 40s to low 
50s; mid 50s for the Champlain Valley and southern Vermont. A few 
sheltered locations could fall as low as the low 40s in portions of 
the Adirondacks with strong radiational cooling. Patchy river fog in 
the Connecticut River and sheltered river valleys of the Adirondacks 
and eastern Vermont will be possible near sunrise tomorrow morning. 

Clouds will increase from southeast to northwest in Vermont, with 
some clearing hanging on across the St. Lawrence Valley by tomorrow 
afternoon. Temperatures will be fairly similar to today; about a 
degree or two warmer with highs in the mid 70s to near 80. More 
southeasterly light breezes, especially in the Champlain Valley are 
expected as another coastal low rides up the East Coast by mid to 
late Saturday. Saturday night lows will be a bit warmer with less 
fog and radiational cooling from increased cloud cover, with values 
in the mid to upper 50s in the higher terrain, and low 60s in the 
Champlain and St. Lawrence Valleys. Precipitation chances begin to 
slowly increase late Saturday night as the coastal low departs to 
the east, and an approaching Great Lakes Trough slides east into 
northern New York.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Following a calm start to the weekend, conditions will 
turn more wet and showery by the latter portion of the weekend. As 
high pressure drifts to the northwest, it will leave in its wake an 
area of subsidence and subtle ridging centered from northeast to 
southwest across Vermont Saturday and Sunday. A pair of systems will 
split this area of ridging bringing shower chances to portions of 
the area. The first of the two systems will be a weak coastal low 
along the coast of southern New England, which will track near Cape 
Cod and is expected to continue moving northeast out into the Gulf 
of Maine. Some showers may be possible in eastern Windsor and Orange 
Counties Saturday night, however, recent trends have suggested 
steadier precipitation associated with the coastal system will stay 
east of the Connecticut River. Any showers that do develop in 
southeastern Vermont will be light in nature. 

The second, higher confidence, system will be an approaching long 
wave trough that will track east from the Great Lakes region. The 
trough translates east into the St. Lawrence Valley late Saturday 
into early Sunday, with scattered rounds of showers. The trough 
slowly tracks east through the day Sunday reaching Vermont by late 
Sunday into Sunday night. While an isolated rumble of thunder with 
the shower activity cannot be ruled out, especially if an earlier 
shower can tap into better diurnal instability, chances are 
relatively low with poor mid level lapse rates, cool surface 
temperatures, and a lack of true instability. In all likelihood, the 
boundary will be a mess of scattered to isolated showers with some 
breaks in between, focused mainly over northern New York, and 
somewhat weakening as it moves east. Between both systems during the 
day Saturday, and most of Sunday, Vermont will be straddled between 
in a "no mans land" of dry and cloudy conditions. Chances for 
showers do not increase for Vermont until Sunday afternoon, though 
some isolated sprinkles or mist will be possible, especially in the 
higher terrain, due to low to mid level stratus clouds. 
Precipitation amounts will be light and have trended down in recent 
model runs, with probabilities of half an inch now below 50%. The 
higher amounts around a quarter inch will be in northern New York, 
primarily in the northern St. Lawrence Valley, and the spine of the 
Greens. The trough will pull away to the northeast heading towards 
Monday. As the trough occludes and drifts northeast, the parent 
upper low will continue to keep showers chances around with wrap 
around cyclonic flow. Clouds and shower chances near the 
International Border and northern New York will continue through the 
day Monday with seasonable temperatures in the low to mid 70s.

next week, with several chances for showers possible. As the upper 
level trough from this weekend exits the region, a few lingering 
showers will be possible into Tuesday, particularly across the
